title: Moores Lab AI’s Benchmark Push: Measuring Whether AI Can Actually Verify Chips
gist: Moores Lab AI is launching a public verification benchmark that scores AI verification environments on whether they detect known hidden bugs, after reporting 93% on an adjusted 56-problem subset of NVIDIA's CVDP; Nenni cautions that the number is subset-specific, that the whole agent workflow must be compared, and that pilots on internal designs should drive purchase decisions.

insights.claim: Moores Lab AI plans a public benchmark where users run their verification environments against designs containing known hidden bugs and are scored on which defects they detect, not on whether testbenches compile or run.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Shifts AI-EDA evaluation from code generation to bug-finding outcomes; a better yardstick for buyers.

insights.claim: Moores Lab AI CEO Shelly Henry argues verification is about finding RTL bugs, protocol correctness, corner cases, assertions and coverage, not writing compiling code.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: AI verification tools should be judged on defect detection, not output volume.
insights.quote: verification is about much more than just writing a compiling code. It’s about finding RTL bugs.

insights.claim: A hidden-defect benchmark's strength depends on whether the seeded bugs are representative, cover meaningful failure modes, and whether correct designs pass without excessive false alarms.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Scrutinise bug realism and false-positive rates before trusting benchmark results.

insights.claim: Moores Lab AI reported a 93% overall pass rate on a selected verification subset of NVIDIA's CVDP benchmark and 100% for stimulus generation, with one attempt per problem in a container using a commercial simulator and hidden graders.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Strong headline number for an AI verification startup, but read the methodology.

insights.claim: Moores Lab AI excluded 6 of 62 CVDP subset problems, saying their hidden graders contradicted the requirements, so the 93% applies to a 56-problem adjusted subset, not the full CVDP benchmark.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Discount vendor benchmark claims that rely on curated subsets.

insights.claim: Si2 is adopting NVIDIA's CVDP into its LLM Benchmarking Coalition, extending categories and refining metrics, which could standardise AI chip-design tool comparisons.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Industry-standard benchmarks will make AI EDA vendor claims more comparable.

insights.claim: When comparing AI verification agents, buyers should compare full configurations, including simulator access, context, iteration limits and compute budgets, because apparent model advantages may reflect the evaluation environment.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Agent workflow, not just base model, drives AI-EDA performance; normalise setups in vendor bake-offs.

insights.claim: AI-generated verification code can look convincing while checking the wrong behavior, and invented requirements can propagate into scoreboards and tests, producing misleading passes.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: False confidence from AI testbenches is a key silicon-respin risk.

insights.claim: Engineering managers should use benchmarks to guide pilots, measuring detected and missed bugs, false positives, engineer intervention, runtime, cost and artifact maintainability on representative internal designs.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Adoption of AI verification tools will be pilot-driven, lengthening sales cycles for vendors.
